assessment.nobel_worthiness: A theoretically predicted flat-band mechanism (the continuum moire model) was followed by an experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle. It created an entire field of tunable correlated matter. This is the clean-model-meets-experiment pattern I value: a simple, general mechanism with large downstream impact across condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald 2011 theory identified the magic angle and flat bands; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 experiments. Pairing theory with experiment is natural. Other groups (for example Dean and colleagues with hBN-aligned devices) contributed soon afterwards, and who else deserves credit (e.g. earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and the Cao et al. co-authors) is unresolved within the supplied names. I recall this from background knowledge and have not verified it.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many independent groups across graphene and other moire systems, with a rapidly maturing literature. The origin of the superconductivity is still debated, but the discovery of the flat-band correlated phases is robust. Timing looks ripe.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled.
Credit beyond the three named people (earlier theory, co-authors on the 2018 papers) is contested.
MacDonald and Bistritzer share one theory paper, so a three-person split must weigh theory against experiment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators opened topological band theory as a unifying classification of matter. It is a simple, general and rigorously analysable idea that was experimentally confirmed and has spread across materials, photonics and cold atoms.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theory of the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene. Molenkamp's group provided the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The credit for BHZ (not in the supplied names) and for 3D topological insulators (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hasan and others) is a real allocation problem. I recall this from background knowledge only.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: decades of independent confirmation by ARPES and transport, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is arguably overdue, apart from the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions which covered the earlier Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz line.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should centre on 2D quantum spin Hall or 3D topological insulators.
Zhang/Bernevig/Hughes (BHZ) and the 3D-TI authors are outside the supplied names, so the list may under-credit decisive contributors.
Overlap with the 2016 prize could make the committee cautious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KPZ equation is a paradigm of non-equilibrium statistical physics, defining a universality class for growth and interface roughening that connects to random matrices, integrable systems and stochastic processes. It is central to my own field and has produced exact solutions and a striking quantitative experimental test (Takeuchi's liquid-crystal turbulence experiments with Tracy-Widom statistics).
assessment.attribution: Kardar, Parisi and Zhang wrote the original 1986 paper; Parisi already received the 2021 prize but for a different body of work and is not in the supplied names. Takeuchi is credited for the experimental confirmation, while the exact solutions (Sasamoto-Spohn, Amir-Corwin-Quastel, Johansson) are theoretical contributions by others not listed. Three credited names is therefore a defensible but incomplete configuration, and the mathematical side may deserve separate recognition.
assessment.maturity: Theory is decades old and is now confirmed in several independent systems, with exact results. The universality is well understood, though some experimental systems (e.g. some interface experiments) show deviations. Timing is fair but not urgent.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Parisi from the credited names is a fairness question that I cannot resolve from the list.
Mathematical exact solutions are credited to others who are not listed.
The scope is narrower than the broader physics prizes of the past decade; breadth of impact beyond statistical physics is moderate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model and the superfluid to Mott insulator transition under full control, and made quantum simulation of many-body systems a working tool. This is statistical mechanics with tunable parameters and direct links to condensed-matter theory.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch-Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner et al. observed the Mott transition in 2002 with Hansch and Bloch; Esslinger did fermionic work. A three-person division among Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is plausible but leaves Esslinger, Jaksch and Hansch/Kasevich-type contributions out. I recall this from background knowledge only.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely replicated. Quantum simulation has since moved to quantum gas microscopes, but the foundational results are stable. Related areas (BEC 2001, Aspect-Clauser-Zeilinger 2022) have already been recognised, so some neighbouring credit has been spent.
uncertainties: Proximity to previous AMO prizes and the 2025 circuit prize.
Esslinger and Jaksch are omitted in a three-person selection.
The scientific question of how much quantum simulation has outperformed classical methods is still open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory turned the infinite-dimension limit of Hubbard-type models into a controlled, widely used non-perturbative method for correlated electrons (Mott transition, heavy fermions). It is a clean analytical idea of the kind I trust, with real predictive power.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the large-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar mapped it onto a quantum impurity problem, and Muller-Hartmann also contributed. Credit is fairly compact, but Metzner and the late Muller-Hartmann are not both listed, and the Georges-Kotliar 1992 paper is the usual centre. The listed trio omits Metzner. I recall this from background knowledge only.
assessment.maturity: Established for about three decades and used daily in materials modelling (DFT+DMFT). Its physical validity is limited by neglected nonlocal correlations, which is well known and not disqualifying.
uncertainties: Approximate method; the finite-dimension error is not controlled.
Omission of Walter Metzner and the death of Muller-Hartmann complicate attribution.
Theory prizes for methodology are rare.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The jamming transition framed the rigidity of disordered matter (foams, grains, glasses) as a critical point with universal scaling. It is a simple unifying picture for soft matter with real experimental and numerical support, and fits the search for universal mechanisms in messy systems.
assessment.attribution: Liu and Nagel's 1998 proposal and the subsequent work of O'Hern, Silbert, Langer and Nagel are the core. Two laureates is a clean configuration, but the contribution of the numerical-scaling collaborators (O'Hern, Silbert, Langer, Wyart) and the mean-field theory of the jamming point (Parisi, Zamponi, Charbonneau) is not captured. This is based on background knowledge and I cannot verify it here.
assessment.maturity: Concept is influential, but details (critical exponents, the relation to glass transition, the role of dimension) are still being tested. Recognition is likely a few years early compared with better-settled topics.
uncertainties: Universality and the nature of the transition are still debated.
Limited direct technological or cross-field impact.
Mean-field replica theory credited elsewhere (Parisi already honoured).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson confirmed the mechanism for electroweak symmetry breaking and completed the Standard Model, a major discovery of the century. The experimental feat of two giant detectors independently reaching the same result is unmatched.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize recognised theory (Englert and Higgs). The experimental credit is spread over thousands of collaborators; Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are founders and project leaders of ATLAS and CMS, but the prize rules and the committee's historic caution about leadership-based credit make this configuration contested. Names such as spokespeople at the time of discovery (Gianotti, Incandela) and accelerator leaders (Evans) are not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed, with independent measurements of couplings that continue to refine it. Recognition has not been given for the experimental side, and the timing is mature, though the Higgs prize was in a sense given in 2013.
uncertainties: Attribution to three founders versus the collaborations or the accelerator builders is highly contested.
The Nobel committee tends to avoid large-collaboration leader awards.
Higgs-related prize was already given in 2013.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and have become the basis of the redefinition of the second and of tests of fundamental physics and geodesy. The magic-wavelength idea is simple, general and experimentally decisive.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock in 2001-2003, and Ye's group brought it to the highest precision with strontium. Two laureates form a compact configuration. The Hall-Hansch 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb, so credit here relates to the clock itself. Other groups (Lemonde, Schiller, Wineland's ion clocks) are not credited. Based on my background knowledge only.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many national metrology institutes have independent optical lattice clocks, and the redefinition of the second is in progress. The thorium nuclear clock is a possible further step but is not necessary for this prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 prize and with the broader precision-metrology field.
Exact credit between Katori and Ye, and with ion-clock pioneers, may be debated.
Impact on fundamental physics is still prospective.
